Sources of Jurisdiction (verbatim): ITU derives its mandate from the Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf) and the Convention of the International Telecommunication Union, which is an international treaty signed and ratified by almost all countries of the world (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Convention-E.pdf). Also, The ITU Constitution and Convention are complemented by the Administrative Regulations, which comprise the ITU International Telecommunication Regulations and ITU Radio Regulations, and are binding on all ITU member states as well (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/RegulationsCollection.aspx#:~:text=ITU's%20Administrative%20Regulations%20contain%20provisions,operation%20of%20international%20telecommunication%20services).

Similarly, the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), which came into effect on September 24, 1960, define the purposes and functions of the IDA, the resources and management of the IDA, the terms and conditions of financing by the IDA, the operations and transactions of the IDA, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IDA. The IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf), which came into effect on July 20, 1956, define the purposes and functions of the IFC, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans, guarantees, and other operations of the IFC, the operations and transactions of the IFC, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IFC. The MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), which came into force on April 12, 1988, defines the purposes and functions of the MIGA, the membership and capital of the MIGA, the guarantees and other operations of the MIGA, the relations with other international organizations, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the MIGA. Lastly, the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf), which entered into force on October 14, 1966, defines the purposes and functions of the ICSID, the jurisdiction of the ICSID, the recognition and enforcement of awards, the administrative and financial provisions of the ICSID, the amendment and interpretation of the ICSID Convention, and the final provisions of the ICSID Convention.
The WBG’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Boards of Governors, the Boards of Executive Directors, and the Council of Governors (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership). Institution: United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA)
Sources of Jurisdiction (verbatim): UNOOSA derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959, which established the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and its secretariat, later renamed as UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the objectives and functions of COPUOS. Additionally, UNOOSA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and principles, such as the five treaties and five declarations on outer space, which provide the legal framework for UNOOSA's jurisdiction over the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html). The five treaties on outer space are: (1) The Outer Space Treaty (1967) on the Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introouterspacetreaty.html), (2) The Rescue Agreement (1968) on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introrescueagreement.html), (3) The Liability Convention (1972) on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introliability-convention.html), (4) The Registration Convention (1976) on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introregistration-convention.html), and (5) The Moon Agreement (1984) governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/intromoon-agreement.html). UNOOSA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by COPUOS and the General Assembly, such as the Space2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which provide guidance and direction for UNOOSA's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/resolutions.html).
